lead: Newton's second law for a flowing fluid says the net force on a chosen control volume equals the rate at which momentum leaves minus the rate at which it enters. The same idea with a moment arm gives torque. This chapter applies the steady linear and angular momentum equations to pipe bends, nozzles, sudden enlargements and sprinklers. These tools size pipe supports, thrust blocks and nozzle anchors, and they check forces that Bernoulli alone cannot give.
prereq: You need Reynolds transport theorem and the continuity equation from Unit 2.

blocks.text: Choose a control volume (CV), a fixed region in space. The fluid inside changes with time, but the CV boundary stays put. Reynolds transport theorem with property velocity V gives the force equation. For steady flow the time derivative vanishes.

blocks.where: ΣF is the vector sum of forces on the fluid in the CV, in N; ṁ is mass flow rate in kg/s; ρ is density in kg/m³; Q is volume flow rate in m³/s; V₁ and V₂ are mass-average velocities at inlet and outlet in m/s.

blocks.text: The forces are of three kinds. Pressure acts on every cut surface of the CV. Body force, usually weight, acts on the fluid mass. Reaction from a solid wall acts where the fluid touches the bend, vane or nozzle. The equation uses components: ΣFx = ṁ(V2x − V1x), and likewise for y and z.

items: Net force is on the fluid, not on the pipe.
Outflow momentum is positive; inflow momentum is negative.
At an inlet, pressure force points opposite the outward normal; for flow in +x at an inlet, pA acts in +x.

blocks.text: A common check: if velocity does not change, as in a straight pipe of constant area, the momentum flux term is zero. Then ΣF = 0, so pressure forces and wall force balance. This is why a straight pipe support carries little axial force from steady flow, while a bend support carries a large one.

For a pipe bend, draw the CV from section 1 to section 2, cutting the pipe. Use continuity to get V₁ = Q/A₁ and V₂ = Q/A₂. If pressures are not given, use Bernoulli when losses are neglected. Write x and y momentum. Solve for the wall force on the fluid. Reverse its sign to report the force of the fluid on the bend.

items: Mark inlet 1 and outlet 2, choose +x and +y, and list p₁A₁ and p₂A₂ with arrows.
Compute A, V, ṁ = ρQ, and each momentum flux ρQV.
Write ΣFx = ṁ(V2x − V1x) and ΣFy = ṁ(V2y − V1y).
Find wall force on fluid, then multiply by −1 for force on the bend.

blocks.text: A nozzle accelerates fluid. The pressure force at the inlet is large and points downstream; the nozzle wall pushes back. The thrust on the nozzle is not just ρQV₂; the pressure term p₁A₁ usually dominates. A sudden enlargement slows the fluid. Momentum gives the pressure rise on the downstream face, while Bernoulli would overpredict it because of losses. The drag on a body can be measured from the momentum defect in its wake: the force equals the rate at which axial momentum is missing downstream, ρ∫u(V − u)dA, where V is the free-stream speed, u the local axial velocity in the wake, and dA a small area of the wake section.

blocks.where: ΣT is torque on the fluid in N·m; r is position vector from the chosen axis in m; V is velocity in m/s; × is vector cross product; the sign follows the right-hand rule.

blocks.text: Angular momentum per unit mass is r × V. Its rate of change equals torque. Only the tangential component of velocity contributes to torque about an axis, because the radial component is parallel to r. For a rotor, the torque on the fluid is positive when the fluid leaves with more angular momentum than it enters.

Lawn sprinkler: water enters at the centre with no angular momentum and leaves one nozzle at radius r = 0.15 m with tangential speed V = 4 m/s. With Q = 0.001 m³/s and ρ = 1000 kg/m³, T = ρQrV = 1000 × 0.001 × 0.15 × 4 = 0.6 N·m. The water gains this torque; the sprinkler arm feels 0.6 N·m in the opposite direction and turns. For an accelerating control volume, only a few syllabi ask for the extra local term ∂/∂t ∫ρV dV and relative velocities; the steady equations above cover most machines and pipe problems.

examples.question: Water flows at Q = 0.1 m³/s through a horizontal 90° reducing bend. The inlet diameter is D₁ = 20 cm and the outlet diameter is D₂ = 10 cm. The outlet discharges to atmosphere. Neglect losses. Find the force of the water on the bend as a vector, its magnitude, and its angle to the inlet axis. Take ρ = 1000 kg/m³.
steps: Bernoulli from 1 to 2, horizontal and p₂ = 0: p₁/ρ + V₁²/2 = 0 + V₂²/2, so p₁ = ρ(V₂² − V₁²)/2 = 500(162.11 − 10.13) = 75,990.9 Pa.
Let inlet velocity be +x and outlet velocity be +y. Wall force on fluid plus pressure at inlet: Fx + p₁A₁ = ṁ(0 − V₁) = 1000×0.1×(−3.183) = −318.3 N.
In y: Fy = ṁ(V₂ − 0) = 1000×0.1×12.732 = 1273.2 N. No outlet pressure term because p₂ = 0.
These are forces of the wall on the fluid. Reverse signs for force of water on bend: (2705.6, −1273.2) N.
Magnitude = √(2705.6² + 1273.2²) = 2990.2 N. Angle = tan⁻¹(1273.2/2705.6) = 25.2° below the inlet axis.
examples.answer: The water exerts 2705.6 N in the inlet direction and 1273.2 N opposite the outlet direction, magnitude 2990.2 N, at 25.2° below the inlet axis.
examples.check:
import math
Q = 0.1
D1 = 0.20
D2 = 0.10
rho = 1000.0
A1 = math.pi * D1**2 / 4.0
A2 = math.pi * D2**2 / 4.0
V1 = Q / A1
V2 = Q / A2
p1 = rho * (V2**2 - V1**2) / 2.0
Fx_wall = -rho * Q * V1 - p1 * A1
Fy_wall = rho * Q * V2
Fx_bend = -Fx_wall
Fy_bend = -Fy_wall
mag = math.sqrt(Fx_bend**2 + Fy_bend**2)
ang = math.degrees(math.atan(abs(Fy_bend / Fx_bend)))
print(round(Fx_bend, 1))
print(round(Fy_bend, 1))
print(round(mag, 1))
print(round(ang, 1))

traps: Leaving out pressure forces p₁A₁ and p₂A₂ on the cut pipe sections. In a nozzle or reducing bend these often exceed the momentum-flux term.
Using Q in place of ṁ = ρQ, which gives an answer in m⁴/s² instead of newtons.
Reporting the force of the wall on the fluid as the force on the bend. Reverse both components.
For a bend, writing the momentum change in only one direction. A 90° bend has a flux in both x and y.
Putting the pressure force in the wrong direction. At an inlet, pA acts opposite the outward normal, which is often downstream.

quiz.q: Write the steady linear momentum equation for a control volume and define each symbol.
quiz.a: ΣF = ṁ(V₂ − V₁); ΣF is net force on fluid in CV (N), ṁ = ρQ mass flow rate (kg/s), V₁ and V₂ inlet and outlet velocities (m/s).

quiz.q: Why must pressure forces on the cut surfaces be included when finding the force on a nozzle?
quiz.a: The cut surfaces are part of the CV boundary. The upstream fluid pushes on the CV with pA; this force changes momentum. In a nozzle p₁A₁ is large and cannot be omitted.

quiz.q: A horizontal 90° bend of constant diameter is fitted at the end of a pipe and discharges freely to atmosphere, so p₁ ≈ p₂ ≈ 0 and pressure forces are negligible. Water flows with Q = 0.02 m³/s at 2 m/s. Find the momentum-flux force of the water on the bend.
quiz.a: ρQV = 1000×0.02×2 = 40 N. Inlet +x, outlet +y. Wall on fluid = (−40, +40) N. Water on bend = (+40, −40) N, magnitude 56.6 N, 45° below inlet axis.

quiz.q: A 90° reducing bend shows a measured support force much larger than ρQV. Explain the missing term.
quiz.a: The area decreases, so V₂ > V₁ and Bernoulli makes p₁ > p₂. The pressure force p₁A₁ on the inlet acts on the CV, and p₂A₂ also acts if p₂ is not zero. These pressure terms add to the momentum-flux term. The support must carry their resultant.

quiz.q: A sprinkler nozzle at r = 0.15 m discharges water tangentially at 4 m/s. Q = 0.001 m³/s, ρ = 1000 kg/m³. Find torque on the water.
In ΣT = ṁ(r₂×V₂ − r₁×V₁), why does only the tangential velocity component produce torque about an axis?
quiz.a: The cross product r×V uses the component of V perpendicular to r. A radial component is parallel to r, so its cross product with r is zero.

quiz.q: What extra terms appear when the control volume itself accelerates, or when the flow is unsteady?
quiz.a: For unsteady flow the local term ∂/∂t ∫ρV dV is added to the surface flux. For a control volume accelerating with a_cv, velocities are taken relative to the CV and the extra term m_cv·a_cv appears, where m_cv is the mass of fluid inside the CV; it acts like a pseudo-force −m_cv·a_cv on the force side of the equation. Steady flow in a fixed CV drops both.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, pipe bend and nozzle support loads are checked with the momentum equation before Civils design thrust blocks. CFD codes solve the same control-volume balances on millions of cells. Rockets use the angular and linear forms for thrust vector control; sprinkler and reaction turbine design uses the angular form.
